edition.editorialNote: Prioritise new developments and material updates. Treat allegations and projections as attributed, and distinguish reported plans from confirmed outcomes.

content.headline: Nvidia investigation questions mount as Trump’s role in Huang’s return draws Scr
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia scrutiny grows over Trump’s role in Huang’s return
content.standfirst: The US attorney general declined to clarify whether Nvidia is under federal investigation, as lawmakers press for answers about the company’s China-linked chip sales and President Donald Trump’s intervention to bring back Jensen Huang.

image.caption: Nvidia’s response to Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive.

sources.originalTitle: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
Schumer accuses Huang of violating US export control laws amid shipments of chips to China
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’
With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
Tech sell-off resumes as euphoria from Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return subsides
‘The mistake has been corrected’: end of Jensen Huang’s brief walk in the wilderness
Medier afdækker magtspillet bag kulisserne: Sådan fik Jensen Huang sit job tilbage
Din pension bliver stadigvæk investeret i Nvidia trods massiv kritik

segments.body: Attorney General Todd Blanche called Nvidia a “good corporate citizen” but declined to say whether the Justice Department or FBI had investigated the company or Huang. Lawmakers are seeking details of Trump’s role in the board’s decision to reinstate Huang and of potential export-control violations involving chips allegedly diverted to China.

segments.title: Questions over the board’s decision
segments.body: Huang is expected to face questioning in Congress next week. Reporting describes bipartisan demands for scrutiny of the company’s China-related sales and the administration’s involvement; the allegations have not been resolved. Nvidia shares fell nearly 6% on Tuesday after surging more than 30% following Huang’s return.

perspectives.body: A DR account, drawing on other outlets’ interviews with anonymous sources, describes lobbying by Silicon Valley figures and officials including Vice-President JD Vance before Huang’s return. A Danish tech correspondent argues that the episode raises concerns about tech companies’ influence over government.

content.headline: Leaked Russian records point to at least 490,000 military deaths in Ukraine war
content.shortHeadline: Leaked records suggest at least 490,000 Russian war deaths
content.standfirst: BBC Russian’s analysis of leaked government mortality data estimates at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the invasion began. The files are incomplete, and Russia does not publish an updated official military toll.

image.caption: A memorial to Russian soldiers killed in the war.

sources.originalTitle: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine

segments.body: BBC Russian and Mediazona matched leaked Rosstat records against independently documented military deaths and identified at least 490,334 Russian soldiers killed since 2022. The dataset contains more than 11 million death records and shows the war’s toll among young men and in particular regions, but the estimate depends on analysis of incomplete records.

segments.title: What the data can—and cannot—show
segments.body: The records were obtained after a cyberattack that Russia’s statistics agency acknowledged, while denying protected information had been leaked. BBC Russian says its own count of confirmed deaths is 290,012 and that the real toll is likely higher. Experts cited by the BBC estimate that its open-source count may represent 45–55% of actual deaths; estimates of Ukrainian losses vary widely.

content.headline: US plans new tariffs on China, EU and other major trading partners
content.shortHeadline: US plans new tariffs on China, EU and other partners
content.standfirst: The White House is expected to announce new import taxes on at least 14 jurisdictions on Wednesday, following a trade investigation. The proposed rates would vary according to deals struck with President Trump.

image.caption: Tariffs have been a signature policy of President Trump’s administration.

sources.originalTitle: US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners

segments.body: The United States is preparing new tariffs on at least 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union and Japan, the BBC reports. The plans follow a so-called Section 301 investigation launched after the Supreme Court ruled Trump’s earlier tariffs illegal. The rates would differ according to agreements each jurisdiction has made with the president.

segments.title: Trade tensions remain
segments.body: The announcement could add strain to US-China trade relations. The two countries have not resolved their dispute, and an interim agreement is due to expire on 10 January. China has extended the suspension of restrictions on exports of several critical minerals until 27 January. The administration’s tariff policy has been criticised for raising consumer prices and harming the global economy.

content.headline: About 20 people remain hostages after armed group seizes Colombian supermarket
content.shortHeadline: About 20 hostages remain after Colombia supermarket seizure
content.standfirst: An armed group reportedly took about 30 people hostage in a Cartagena supermarket after attempting to seize an armoured cash vehicle. Authorities say ten have been released; the operation was continuing at the time of the report.

image.caption: Armed police stand outside the supermarket in Cartagena.

sources.originalTitle: 20 personer fortsat holdt fanget i gidseldrama i Colombia

segments.body: About 20 people were still being held after armed men took control of a supermarket in Cartagena, Colombian authorities said, according to AP. The group had reportedly first tried to seize an armoured vehicle carrying cash from a shopping centre. Ten hostages, including five older women, had been released, Reuters reported.

segments.title: Broader security concerns
segments.body: The hostage-taking came amid a reported rise in attacks by armed groups against government targets. A car bomb in Villavicencio injured more than 20 people and damaged about 500 properties, according to local authorities. No one had claimed responsibility for the bombing; the president blamed dissidents from the former FARC guerrilla group.

content.headline: Iowa prepares controlled blast of five tonnes of explosives amid lead concerns
content.shortHeadline: Iowa braces for controlled blast of five tonnes of explosives
content.standfirst: The US Army plans to detonate degraded explosives on Wednesday, saying a controlled blast is safer than leaving them in place. Residents have been advised to evacuate or shelter indoors, while some fear lead dust could affect farms and water.

image.caption: The US Army has prepared defences for the planned Iowa explosives detonation.

sources.originalTitle: 'This could be apocalyptic' - Iowans hunker down for controlled blast of explosives stockpile

segments.body: The Army plans to detonate 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant after an appeals court overturned a decision to stop the blast. Officials have set an optional evacuation zone extending five miles and advised people within 20 miles to shelter in place. The Army says the explosives pose a growing risk of an accidental explosion as temperatures fall.

segments.title: Local concerns and uncertainty
segments.body: Some residents fear airborne lead dust could affect farms and water; the Army has warned the plume could travel as far as 100 miles, depending on wind and weather. Others near the plant say they would rather see a controlled detonation than risk an unplanned explosion. Residents and local officials have also criticised the information provided and the uncertainty about the aftermath.

content.headline: North Korean defectors describe surveillance, beatings and prison over Christian
content.shortHeadline: North Korean defectors describe persecution for their Christian faith
content.standfirst: A report based on interviews with 570 escapees documents accounts of surveillance, imprisonment and violence against people suspected of practising Christianity. North Korea says it allows religious freedom; the cases in the report are testimonies, not independently verified findings.

image.caption: North Korea’s government is accused of suppressing religious freedom.

sources.originalTitle: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian

segments.body: A new report by the human rights group Korea Future records the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom said they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution. One interviewee, Kim Bo-bin, told the BBC she was beaten and sentenced to hard labour after being deported from China. The BBC says her account matches other testimonies in the report.

segments.title: Faith under state control
segments.body: The report describes a system of surveillance and punishment for unauthorised religious activity, including owning Bibles or sharing religious materials. North Korea maintains that it permits religious freedom, but the BBC reports that churches in Pyongyang are controlled by the state. The report’s authors say the testimonies suggest little has changed despite international pressure.

content.headline: Huawei guilty of trade-secret theft conspiracy, acquitted of racketeering
content.shortHeadline: Huawei convicted on trade-secret and bank-fraud counts
content.standfirst: A US jury found the Chinese technology company guilty on 10 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but rejected a racketeering charge. Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027, and Huawei says it expects to appeal.

image.caption: Huawei’s defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments in the case.

sources.originalTitle: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering

segments.body: A jury in Brooklyn found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but did not convict the company of racketeering. Prosecutors alleged it lied to banks about business in Iran and stole technology from rival firms. Huawei’s defence argued the case wrongly portrayed the company as a criminal enterprise.

segments.title: Appeal expected
segments.body: The case began with charges announced in 2019 and followed the arrest in Canada of senior executive Meng Wanzhou, who was later released under a deal with US prosecutors. Huawei said the racketeering acquittal showed that allegations lacked a factual basis; its lawyer said the company expects to appeal the convictions. Sentencing is planned for September 2027.

content.headline: Pakistan’s first astronaut joins Chinese mission to Tiangong space station
content.shortHeadline: Pakistani astronaut joins China’s mission to Tiangong
content.standfirst: Pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is the first foreign astronaut to take part in a Chinese space mission and the first non-Chinese citizen to visit the Tiangong station. He is expected to conduct experiments during a five-day mission.

image.caption: Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Chinese crewmates at a departure ceremony.

sources.originalTitle: Kina sender for første gang en udenlandsk astronaut på rummission

segments.body: China launched three astronauts toward its Tiangong space station aboard the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft, according to Chinese state media cited by AFP. The crew includes Pakistani air force pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first non-Chinese astronaut to take part in a Chinese mission and visit the station.

segments.title: A five-day mission
segments.body: Ali is expected to conduct experiments, including studying how quinoa seeds respond to spaceflight, according to Pakistan’s space agency. The mission is expected to last five days. China aims to send astronauts to the Moon by 2030, as the United States pursues its Artemis programme.

content.headline: Met still institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic, review finds
content.shortHeadline: Review finds discrimination persists in the Metropolitan Police
content.standfirst: An independent review says systemic problems remain three years after a major inquiry into the force’s culture. It cites accounts of retaliation fears, poor treatment of victims and weak progress on earlier recommendations; the commissioner accepts the recommendations but disputes some labels.

image.caption: Mayor of London Sadiq Khan commissioned the review of the Metropolitan Police.

sources.originalTitle: Metropolitan police still institutionally racist and misogynist, says report
Latest review of Met police culture finds little has changed since last one

segments.body: An independent review led by Gillian Fairfield found that institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia remain in the Metropolitan Police, with “fundamental, systemic issues” and deep-rooted defensiveness. It said the force had not made good progress on any of the 14 recommendations from the 2023 Casey review, though it had made some progress in nine areas and limited progress in five.

segments.title: Concerns over accountability and trust
segments.body: The review describes officers fearing retaliation if they report misconduct and victims’ families feeling they were blamed or misled. It says only 44% of Met staff felt confident raising concerns about a senior officer. Commissioner Mark Rowley accepted the recommendations but said he would not be drawn into what he called a politicised debate over labels; he said the force was confronting discrimination.

The review warns that further scandals are highly likely unless the force addresses cultures in areas including specialist protection and custody. Mayor Sadiq Khan said the Met must acknowledge institutional discrimination to change its culture. The report also recognises some improvements, including in vetting and misconduct processes, while finding confidence in them remains uneven.

content.headline: Proposed PIP overhaul could leave hundreds of thousands without disability
content.shortHeadline: PIP overhaul could cut support for hundreds of thousands
content.standfirst: A government review proposes reshaping England and Wales’s main disability benefit around additional costs and individual needs. Ministers have yet to decide who would qualify under a new test or whether it would affect current claimants.

image.caption: The Timms review recommends assessments tailored to claimants’ circumstances.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of thousands could lose disability benefits under Timms plans for Pip shake-up
What are the proposals for changing personal independence payment?
All PIP changes announced – from fast-track routes to ending unnecessary reviews
The benefit claimants who will be shielded from PIP cuts
UK disability benefit cuts risk worsening youth destitution, research warns
I was a PIP assessor – this is how the system sets people up to fail

segments.body: Stephen Timms has described personal independence payment (PIP) as “no longer fit for purpose” and recommended a new eligibility assessment based on the extra costs and needs associated with disability. The Resolution Foundation estimates that up to one in six claimants—about 666,000 people—say they have no additional costs. No final decision has been made on whether reforms would apply to existing claimants or only new ones.

segments.title: How the review differs from other proposals
segments.body: The review recommends faster awards for people with severe conditions and fewer repeat assessments for those whose conditions are unlikely to improve; the government has accepted those two recommendations. It proposes a more tailored assessment for other claimants, but ministers have not yet decided whether to adopt it. Alan Milburn’s separate review proposed ending PIP for under-25s, a proposal that has prompted concern from campaigners.

segments.title: Concerns about hardship and assessment
segments.body: The Joseph Rowntree Foundation says 3.8 million people experienced destitution in the UK last year and warns that changes to disability benefits could worsen hardship. A former PIP assessor also worries that judging additional costs could be difficult for people who rely on unpaid care or cannot provide receipts.

perspectives.body: Former assessor James Merrell argues that spending records may not show what support someone needs: people may rely on a partner’s care or lack receipts for transport. He fears a cost-focused assessment could make it harder for some disabled people to qualify.

content.headline: UK energy bills forecast to rise 26% in January as new price cap looms
content.shortHeadline: Energy bills forecast to rise 26% under January price cap
content.standfirst: A forecast from Cornwall Insight suggests a typical annual bill could rise by about £443 to £2,166 if the increase lasts a year. The new cap is due to be announced shortly, and households on fixed tariffs will not be affected until their deal ends.

image.caption: Energy bills are forecast to rise for households on variable tariffs.

sources.originalTitle: Households braced for soaring energy bills with new price cap to be announced

segments.body: A typical household’s energy bill could rise by 26% from January, according to a forecast by Cornwall Insight ahead of Ofgem’s announcement of its new price cap. If sustained for a year, the increase would add about £37 a month and £443 to the annual bill, bringing it to £2,166 for a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity.

segments.title: Support and household debt
segments.body: About 20 million households on variable tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales are exposed to the cap; people on fixed deals are not affected until they renew. The government plans a £100 payment for many households and a £150 Warm Home Discount for eligible people. Citizens Advice warns that prepayment customers may use the support quickly and expects more people to seek emergency help.

The forecast rise is driven mainly by higher wholesale gas prices following the war in Iran, alongside relatively low storage levels. Energy UK says average gas prices are 166% above late last year. The trade body estimates total energy debt could approach £7bn by year’s end, as charities warn that rising bills will leave some households with little money for other essentials.

content.headline: MI5 warns UK firms supplying Ukraine they could face Russian sabotage
content.shortHeadline: MI5 warns firms supporting Ukraine of Russian sabotage risk
content.standfirst: A rare public warning from MI5 and the Ministry of Defence urges defence suppliers and critical infrastructure firms to strengthen security against possible arson, sabotage and intimidation by Russian proxies. The warning does not identify a specific imminent attack.

image.caption: The warning follows reported sabotage attempts targeting European defence facilities.

sources.originalTitle: Alert issued for Russian sabotage and arson attacks on UK sites

segments.body: MI5 and the Ministry of Defence have warned British companies supplying Ukraine that they could be targeted by sabotage, arson and intimidation carried out by Russian proxies. The alert advises firms to improve perimeter security, rehearse responses to attacks and watch for hostile reconnaissance. It also urges them to reduce the digital footprint of critical staff.

segments.title: A wider European threat
segments.body: The warning also applies to companies involved in critical national infrastructure, including data centres. It comes amid reported attacks on defence-related sites in Europe and follows a series of arson cases linked by investigators to Russian intelligence. Security experts cited by the i Paper say the public alert suggests authorities have concrete intelligence, but the report does not specify a particular planned attack.

content.headline: Burnham brings forward changes to NDAs after abuse cases prompt calls for
content.shortHeadline: Burnham advances NDA changes as pressure grows to protect victims
content.standfirst: From January, victims of crime or workplace harassment will have greater freedom to speak despite signing a non-disclosure agreement. Andy Burnham says further steps will follow, including a consultation on a staggered age of consent.

image.caption: The prime minister has promised changes to protections for people affected by abuse.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse

segments.body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says changes to non-disclosure agreements will take effect in January, giving victims of crimes or workplace harassment freedom to speak even if they signed an NDA. He called the measure “just the start” and promised a consultation on a staggered age of consent following recent high-profile cases.

segments.title: Campaigners want wider protections
segments.body: Campaigners say the changes should go further and prevent NDAs being used to silence fans, freelancers and others outside employment. The debate has intensified after allegations of improper behaviour against David Walliams, which he denies, and Russell Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault. The government says it is considering loopholes and exceptions.

content.headline: NHS trusts to face investigation over repeated failures to disclose treatment
content.shortHeadline: Ombudsman to investigate NHS failures to disclose treatment errors
content.standfirst: England’s public service ombudsman says repeated breaches of the duty of candour leave patients and families without answers and can prevent lessons being learned. A report with recommendations is expected next year.

image.caption: NHS trusts must disclose when lapses in care cause death or serious harm.

sources.originalTitle: NHS trusts to be investigated over ‘repeated failures’ to admit treatment errors

segments.body: The public service ombudsman for England, Paula Sussex, is investigating repeated failures by NHS trusts to tell patients or families when treatment errors cause death or harm. The statutory duty of candour was introduced in 2014, but Sussex says trusts’ compliance remains inconsistent and families are too often left to fight for answers.

segments.title: The impact on families
segments.body: In one case examined by Sussex, a 70-year-old woman died after failings at Kettering General Hospital NHS Trust. Her family was not told that staff had raised concerns about her treatment, her daughter said. Sussex says a lack of openness can compound distress and prevent hospitals from learning from mistakes; she plans to make recommendations next year.

content.headline: One in three young adults in Britain have never had sex, survey finds
content.shortHeadline: Survey finds a third of young adults have never had sex
content.standfirst: A national study found more young people have never had sex than in earlier surveys, while many report sexting or watching pornography. Researchers say the findings show changing behaviour but do not establish why it is changing.

sources.originalTitle: Third of young Brits have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn
‘Not about notches on bedpost’: people in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults

segments.body: The latest National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles found that about one in three people aged 16 to 24 have never had sex, up from about one in five in earlier surveys. Among this age group, half reported sending or receiving sexual images in the past year; half of young women and 86% of young men said they had watched pornography.

segments.title: A changing picture, with causes still unclear
segments.body: Across adults under 45, the average reported frequency of sex has fallen from once a week in 1990 to twice a month. Researchers say the survey does not explain the trend; factors may include less drinking, more young adults living with parents, mental health and the pandemic. The study surveyed about 6,700 people across Britain.

The study also found a rise in the proportion of women reporting that they do not want children and a decline in use of the contraceptive pill among young women. Researchers say those trends warrant further investigation; the survey itself cannot determine what is driving them.

content.headline: North Ockendon residents say Reform failed to stop planned mega data centre
content.shortHeadline: Residents accuse Reform of breaking promise over huge data centre
content.standfirst: People in North Ockendon say they backed Reform UK after its local campaign opposed a proposed data centre on greenbelt land. The council says it cannot prevent a private company applying to build, while the project’s opponents cite its expected energy and land demands.

image.caption: North Ockendon resident Karen Fitzgerald campaigned against the proposed data centre.

sources.originalTitle: How plans to build Europe’s biggest data hub in a tiny village left Reform in turmoil

segments.body: Residents of North Ockendon say they feel betrayed after Reform UK took control of Havering Council but did not halt plans for a data centre that could cover 500 acres of greenbelt. A former Conservative councillor who defected to Reform had said the party could cancel the application if elected, according to the i Paper.

segments.title: Local opposition and the council’s position
segments.body: The developer says the project would include a 280-acre ecology park. Residents argue it would not offset the effects of a large facility, which they say could use as much electricity as more than one million households. The council did not respond to the paper’s request for comment; its leader has said it cannot prevent a private company submitting a planning application.

The dispute reflects wider opposition to data centres and the resources required to support them. More than 150 projects are in the UK planning system, according to analysis cited by the paper. Reform has voiced support for Britain’s AI industry but has also backed taking time to consider hyperscale data-centre planning.

content.headline: Frederiksen faces criticism and support-party threat over ‘population replace
content.shortHeadline: Frederiksen under pressure over ‘population replacement’ remark
content.standfirst: The Alternative threatens to withdraw support for the government if the prime minister uses the phrase again. Critics say it echoes a far-right conspiracy theory; Frederiksen rejects that association and says she supports a strict immigration policy.

image.caption: Mette Frederiksen faced criticism from supporting parties during parliamentary questions.

sources.originalTitle: Ét ord har sat Mette Frederiksen under et massivt pres, og nu handler det pludselig også om regeringens fremtid

segments.body: Mette Frederiksen faced renewed criticism after saying she did not support a “large population replacement”. The Alternative says it may be difficult to continue supporting the government if she uses the phrase again. The party’s leader says the term is associated with a far-right conspiracy theory about immigration.

segments.title: The prime minister’s response
segments.body: Frederiksen rejected being linked to conspiracy theorists and said she would not be drawn into a debate about the word. She defended a strict immigration policy and said Denmark needed a strong majority culture. The Social Democrats’ youth organisation also criticised the language, saying it had polarised the debate.

content.headline: Danish Social Democrats’ youth wing says tax deal favours the wealthy
content.shortHeadline: Social Democratic youth wing criticises tax deal as unfair
content.standfirst: The party’s youth organisation says the agreement with the Danish People’s Party offers too little to ordinary wage earners. The government argues that corporate tax cuts will also benefit workers, a claim the youth leader disputes.

image.caption: DSU chair Ingrid Kjærgaard criticises the tax agreement.

sources.originalTitle: Unge socialdemokrater angriber skatteaftale: Svigter almindelige danskere

segments.body: The Social Democrats’ youth organisation, DSU, has criticised the government’s tax agreement with the Danish People’s Party, saying it benefits some of the wealthiest while offering ordinary workers cheaper fuel instead of permanent income-tax relief. DSU chair Ingrid Kjærgaard called the deal disappointing and socially unfair.

The agreement removes the middle and top-top tax rates and cuts corporation tax, while reducing petrol and diesel duties from 1 December and through 2027. The government says workers will also benefit from the corporation tax cut. Kjærgaard disputes that calculation, arguing the direct benefit goes first to companies and people with investment income.

content.headline: Denmark’s third Limfjord link faces DKK 3.5bn cost increase and likely delay
content.shortHeadline: Limfjord road link faces DKK 3.5bn cost rise and delays
content.standfirst: The proposed third connection near Aalborg is now estimated to cost 40% more than expected, with difficult ground and PFAS contamination adding to the bill. Politicians must decide whether to fund the original plan or consider changes.

image.caption: Plan for the third Limfjord connection, now estimated to cost DKK 3.5bn more.

sources.originalTitle: Motorvej bliver flere milliarder kroner dyrere – og højst sandsynligt forsinket
Minister om dyrere motorvejsforbindelse: Beklageligt, men alting stiger

segments.body: The Danish Road Directorate estimates that the planned third Limfjord connection will cost DKK 3.5bn more than expected, putting the original project’s price close to 40% above forecast. It also says the road is likely to be delayed, putting the planned 2035 completion date at risk.

segments.title: Costly ground conditions
segments.body: The Road Directorate cites higher prices for construction materials, difficult ground conditions and additional PFAS contamination. One possible cost-saving change would replace a tunnel south of Egholm with a bridge. The final decision is for politicians; Transport Minister Karina Lorentzen Dehnhardt says the original plan has become much more expensive but continues to back a third connection.

content.headline: Copenhagen Airport neighbours protest expansion as Tårnby approves fuel
content.shortHeadline: Airport neighbours protest as Tårnby backs fuel-system expansion
content.standfirst: More than 200 residents protested in Tårnby over fears of increased air and noise pollution from Copenhagen Airport. A council majority approved an expansion allowing fuel to reach 15 additional aircraft stands; the municipality says it will not cause significant environmental effects under proposed conditions.

image.caption: Residents demonstrate against concerns about Copenhagen Airport’s expansion.

sources.originalTitle: Med mundbind, kampråb og bannere: Naboer til Københavns Lufthavn demonstrerede med opråb til lokalpolitikere

segments.body: More than 200 neighbours of Copenhagen Airport demonstrated outside Tårnby town hall against concerns about future air and noise pollution. Despite local opposition, a council majority approved an expansion to a fuel system serving 15 additional aircraft stands.

segments.title: Disagreement over the impact
segments.body: Campaign spokesperson Louise Raaschou Petersen called the decision a failure to protect residents’ health and said the work could enable a much larger airport expansion. The municipality’s administration assessed that the fuel-system extension would not have a significant environmental impact under proposed conditions. The airport says development should be responsible and respect nearby residents.

content.headline: Danish pension funds keep Nvidia shares despite concerns over governance
content.shortHeadline: Danish pension funds hold Nvidia shares as scrutiny continues
content.standfirst: Five major Danish pension providers say they have no immediate plans to sell their Nvidia holdings while investigations and questions about board independence continue. PFA says it has more than DKK 18bn invested in the company.

image.caption: Danish pension providers say they are not selling their Nvidia shares for now.

sources.originalTitle: Din pension bliver stadigvæk investeret i Nvidia trods massiv kritik

segments.body: Five large Danish pension providers are retaining their Nvidia shares for now despite criticism of the company’s governance and US President Trump’s involvement in Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive. PFA says it has more than DKK 18bn invested in the chipmaker and sees no reason to sell before more facts emerge.

segments.title: Funds cite unresolved questions
segments.body: Danica says it is waiting for investigations into Huang’s conduct and the company’s future chip sales. Velliv says political involvement in a listed company makes investment risks harder to assess, while Nordea and AP Pension say they have not excluded Nvidia and continue to review the investment. Huang is expected to face questions from congressional committees next week.

content.headline: Copenhagen campaign aims to make nightlife safer for young people
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen campaign targets young people’s nightlife safety
content.standfirst: One in four people aged 15 to 29 in Copenhagen say they feel unsafe in the evening or at night, according to the municipality. A new campaign includes expanded late-night access to a youth centre where people can get help.

image.caption: A Copenhagen youth centre is extending its opening hours to support young people at night.

sources.originalTitle: Du er fuld, din telefon er løbet tør for strøm, og du er blevet væk fra dine venner: Kampagne skal hjælpe

segments.body: Copenhagen Municipality says one in four residents aged 15 to 29 feel unsafe in the evening or at night. A new campaign by the municipality, Copenhagen Police and the Danish Crime Prevention Council aims to address common problems, including young people becoming separated from friends.

segments.title: A late-night place to turn
segments.body: The municipality is extending the opening hours of Fairhuset, a youth centre in central Copenhagen. Young people can come in to meet a sober adult, warm up, use a toilet, charge a phone or get help finding friends, says the centre’s manager.

content.headline: Adult adoption gave Christian a stronger sense of belonging to his family
content.shortHeadline: Adopted at 38, Christian says the change meant more than he expected
content.standfirst: A change to Danish rules has made adult adoption easier where a parent-child relationship exists. Christian, who had lived with his adoptive family since childhood, says formalising the bond gave him a stronger sense of belonging.

image.caption: Christian says his adoption formalised the family bond he already felt.

sources.originalTitle: Christian var 38, da han blev adopteret - det har ændret mere, end han troede

segments.body: Christian Thorup Børjesson was adopted by his former foster parents at the age of 38. He had lived with them since he was four, but says the formal adoption still changed how he felt about belonging to the family. His adoptive mother says the relationship now carries the clarity of being able to call him her son.

segments.title: Rules changed in 2025
segments.body: Since the beginning of 2025, adult adoption has been possible where a parent-child-like relationship exists; previously, applicants had to have raised the person before they turned 18. Denmark’s Agency of Family Law received 404 applications in the first six months after the change, roughly the same as before. An adoption counsellor says the need to feel part of a family does not disappear in adulthood.

content.headline: Senegal reinstated as Afcon champions after court overturns title decision
content.shortHeadline: Senegal reinstated as Afcon champions
content.standfirst: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has restored Senegal’s 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title, overturning the ruling that awarded it to Morocco after Senegal’s players left the pitch during the final.

image.caption: Sadio Mané’s Senegal have been reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners.

sources.originalTitle: Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling

segments.body: Senegal are Afcon champions again after CAS ruled unanimously that the final’s result should stand. The team had returned to the pitch after walking off in protest at a penalty decision, then won 1-0 after extra time. A Caf appeals board later overturned that result and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

segments.title: A possible next step
segments.body: Morocco’s football federation said it was surprised by the ruling and would pursue available legal avenues to challenge it. CAS has not yet published the full grounds for its decision; Caf says it will implement the award.

content.headline: Donald and Salt power England to emphatic T20 win over Australia
content.shortHeadline: Donald and Salt put England level with Australia
content.standfirst: A 151-run opening stand helped England chase 184 in just 13.1 overs on the Gold Coast, levelling the five-match series at 1-1 after Australia won the opener.

image.caption: Aneurin Donald struck 85 from 32 balls against Australia.

sources.originalTitle: 'The rest of the world noticed' - Welshman Donald demolishes Aussies

segments.body: Aneurin Donald smashed 85 from 32 balls and Phil Salt made 58 as England reached 188-2 to win by eight wickets. Their opening partnership produced 151 runs in 10 overs; Donald’s 18-ball fifty was the joint third-fastest by an England batter in T20 internationals.

segments.title: A remarkable chase, with work still to do
segments.body: England’s bowlers had let Australia recover to 184-8 after the hosts lost four wickets in the powerplay. Michael Vaughan said Donald’s display would draw attention to his talents, while the report also noted England’s difficulties closing out an innings. The series is level at 1-1.

content.headline: Cherki rescues Manchester City draw as doubts grow over their form
content.shortHeadline: Cherki rescues a point as Man City’s form falters
content.standfirst: Rayan Cherki scored late to earn a 2-2 Champions League draw with Napoli, but Manchester City have won only once in their past seven matches in all competitions inside 90 minutes.

image.caption: Rayan Cherki scored late to earn Manchester City a draw against Napoli.

sources.originalTitle: 'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt

segments.body: Manchester City twice fell behind to Rasmus Højlund and Noa Lang before Cherki rescued a point. City had 62.7% possession and attempted 665 passes, but the reporting described their play as slow and lacking incisiveness. Manager Enzo Maresca said his team created chances and fought to the end.

segments.title: A run of uneven results
segments.body: City have conceded in 10 successive games and have not won any of their past four Premier League matches. Erling Haaland, who has scored 20 goals for club and country this season, has drawn a blank in his past two games; he said he felt he had enough chances against Napoli.

content.headline: Bellingham's wonder volley sparks Real Madrid's 5-1 recovery against PSV
content.shortHeadline: Bellingham sparks Real Madrid’s 5-1 comeback
content.standfirst: Left out of the starting line-up, Jude Bellingham came on at half-time and scored a spectacular volley as Real Madrid turned a 1-0 deficit into a 5-1 Champions League win.

image.caption: Jude Bellingham celebrates after scoring against PSV.

sources.originalTitle: Bellingham plays down Zidane comparison after wonder goal

segments.body: Fede Valverde equalised in the 50th minute before Bellingham’s volley put Real Madrid ahead 10 minutes later. Kylian Mbappé scored twice and Vinícius Júnior added another in the 5-1 win. Manager José Mourinho called Bellingham the world’s best midfielder; Bellingham said he was surprised by the finish and played down comparisons with Zinedine Zidane.

content.headline: Arsenal held by Dortmund after 30 shots, with finishing still a concern
content.shortHeadline: Arsenal held by Dortmund despite 30 shots
content.standfirst: Viktor Gyökeres put Arsenal ahead, but they drew 1-1 with Borussia Dortmund after converting only four of 30 attempts into shots on target. Mikel Arteta said his side needed more luck and better finishing.

image.caption: Viktor Gyökeres scored Arsenal’s goal against Borussia Dortmund.

sources.originalTitle: Arteta says Arsenal need more luck to kill off games

segments.body: Arsenal led at half-time through Gyökeres, but could not turn their pressure into a second goal and were held 1-1. They had 30 shots, four on target; Gyökeres also missed a late header from close range that could have won the match.

segments.title: Arteta sees progress, but wants more
segments.body: The draw continues a recent pattern: Arsenal have won by more than one goal only once in their past nine matches across all competitions. Arteta praised what he called a brilliant performance, while saying the team needed to finish chances better. Arsenal remain unbeaten in this Champions League league phase.

content.headline: United plan to challenge handling of Yoro red card after FA overturns it
content.shortHeadline: Man Utd challenge Yoro red-card decision after reversal
content.standfirst: The FA has overturned Leny Yoro’s early dismissal in Manchester United’s 4-0 loss at Liverpool. Mauricio Pochettino has criticised the VAR process, while referees’ chief Howard Webb defended the call.

image.caption: Referee Sam Barrott shows Manchester United’s Leny Yoro a red card at Anfield.

sources.originalTitle: Pochettino leads Man Utd fury at Yoro red card ruling

segments.body: Yoro was sent off eight minutes into Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, but the FA has since overturned the red card. Manchester United say Aleksander Isak’s heavy touch meant he could not reach the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens; that is the club’s account of the incident.

segments.title: A dispute over the review
segments.body: Pochettino said he was angry that VAR upheld the on-field decision. Referees’ chief Howard Webb said the call was not clearly and obviously wrong, while acknowledging there was a question over whether Isak would have reached the ball. United intend to take the matter up with the Premier League and ProRef.

content.headline: Sinner has minor knee surgery with Australian Open return uncertain
content.shortHeadline: Sinner has knee surgery with Australian Open in view
content.standfirst: The world number two says he had surgery to improve the condition of his iliotibial band after months of treatment without an operation. He hopes to return in time for Australia, but gives no recovery timetable.

sources.originalTitle: 'I miss being on court' - Sinner has 'minor surgery' on knee

segments.body: Jannik Sinner said he had “minor surgery” on his knee after it failed to respond as hoped to non-surgical treatment. The five-time Grand Slam champion has not competed since winning Wimbledon on 12 July and said he would now begin his recovery with his team.

segments.title: Australian Open remains a question
segments.body: Sinner had previously said he hoped to go to Australia and might play some tournaments before the Australian Open begins on 17 January. He has not provided a recovery timeline, and says he is also mindful of protecting his long-term career.

content.headline: Sheehan banned for two games and ruled out of Ireland's Australia Test
content.shortHeadline: Sheehan ban rules him out of Ireland’s Australia Test
content.standfirst: Ireland’s stand-in captain Dan Sheehan has received a two-game ban for a croc-roll tackle against South Africa. He will miss Friday’s Test against Australia and a Leinster match on 4 December.

image.caption: Ireland’s Dan Sheehan has 43 international caps.

sources.originalTitle: Sheehan out of Wallabies Test after two-game ban

segments.body: Sheehan’s yellow card in Ireland’s 20-17 win over South Africa was upgraded to a red by the foul play review officer. A disciplinary panel ruled that the tackle was a low-entry-point offence and imposed a two-week ban, leaving the hooker unavailable for Ireland’s final game of 2026.

segments.title: Another selection change for Ireland
segments.body: Sheehan started at number eight against South Africa, a first in his Test career, but usually plays hooker. His absence adds to Ireland’s options at the base of the scrum already being affected by injuries to Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen.

content.headline: Stella Z turns field recordings and lucid dreams into ambient soundscapes
content.shortHeadline: Stella Z’s ambient dreams draw on recordings from China
content.standfirst: The Fujian-born, London-based producer builds a nocturnal collage from sounds gathered on trips to China. Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming drifts between ambient, dub and acid, with unease sometimes lending its most vivid moments their charge.

image.caption: Stella Z, the Fujian-born, London-based producer.

sources.originalTitle: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming

segments.body: Sounds recorded on Stella Z’s trips to China—among them a pharmacy and the Fujian mountains at night—give Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming its unusual sense of place. Across eight tracks, whispers, percussion and electronics create an unsettled, dreamlike collage.

The album moves through ambient and new-age expanses, with traces of 1990s downtempo, acid and dub. “Exit, Elsewhere” grows disorientating through overlapping narration and rattling bells; a remix by Valentina Magaletti turns the original’s wistfulness into something harsher. Even its clumsier passages help conjure a woozy wilderness.

content.headline: Kate Nash turns music-industry frustration into a fight for touring artists
content.shortHeadline: Kate Nash challenges a music business that makes touring precarious
content.standfirst: The singer’s OnlyFans-funded “Butts for Tour Buses” campaign made the cost of touring hard to ignore. Her forthcoming album Cailín draws on Irish roots, while she argues that fair pay for working musicians requires more than goodwill.

image.caption: Kate Nash.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

segments.body: In 2024, Kate Nash used an OnlyFans account to help fund a tour and staged a protest outside Spotify and Live Nation. She says even artists with established catalogues struggle to make touring work, while friends sell instruments or abandon the road altogether. Without small and mid-sized gigs, she argues, the wider music culture is at risk.

segments.title: A record rooted in family history
segments.body: On Cailín, recorded in Spiddal on Ireland’s west coast, Nash combines traditional instruments with punk and hip-hop as she explores her Irish heritage. The album includes a cover of Sinéad O’Connor’s “Famine”, and follows Nash’s discovery that her grandfather was among men imprisoned while trying to travel to Spain to fight Franco.

segments.title: Making a case for change
segments.body: Nash says the music industry will not reform itself and argues that legislation is needed to make payment fairer. Her account traces the distance between early fame and a career she has rebuilt on her own terms, including acting work and an independent approach to making music.

content.headline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul turn grief into playful, personal pop
content.shortHeadline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul get personal on a new album
content.standfirst: The Belgian duo’s second album, Mainland Madinina, follows a period of grief and becoming parents. Their familiar wit remains, but the new songs also make room for vulnerability, family history and questions about what gets passed on.

image.caption: Bolis Pupul and Charlotte Adigéry.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

segments.body: After the sharp, politically minded pop of their debut, Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul describe their forthcoming album as more introspective. They began writing it after Adigéry’s father died, and worked on early demos during a trip to Martinique, her parents’ birthplace.

segments.title: Humour alongside grief
segments.body: The record still makes room for absurdity: “Googoo Gaga” plays with parenthood, while “From Healer to Dealer” sends up wellness language. But closing song “I’m Lost” turns toward Adigéry’s grief, as she sings about finally throwing away flowers from her father’s funeral. The album also considers how becoming a parent can bring family trauma into focus.

segments.title: Pop as a Trojan horse
segments.body: The duo say they first recognised the political reach of their music when a Manchester crowd sang along to the deliberately provocative chorus of “Blenda”. Their aim, they explain, is to trust listeners to understand the joke and the ideas carried inside the pop.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s debut solo album makes centuries of folk feel immediate
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat brings centuries of folk into the present
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer gathers songs from Irish, British and American traditions, centring complex women’s stories. Her commanding voice anchors arrangements that move from stark folk to a striking trip-hop reworking.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: Radie Peat opens No Human Tongue Can Tell with the traditional “Hares on the Mountain”, her voice coming in before the piano. The Lankum and ØXN singer plays nearly every instrument on this solo debut, building layered choruses around a voice the review describes as an arresting contralto.

segments.title: Songs that speak across time
segments.body: Peat draws on Irish, British and American songbooks, with particular attention to women whose choices are constrained. The tracklist sets older songs alongside more recent compositions, finding connections between a story of abuse and Liam Weldon’s lament for the frustrated promise of Irish independence.

The boldest transformation is “The Moon and Stars”, which turns the archived fiddle tune “Maid Lamenting” into a trip-hop piece with a skittering beat and surging keyboards. Peat’s performance cuts through the dense production, drawing the album’s distant musical eras into a vivid present.

content.headline: Thoom fuses hyperpop and Arabic instrumentation into a volatile debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop collide with Arabic instrumentation
content.standfirst: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, Beirut-born, Los Angeles-based artist Zeynab Marwan puts her voice at the centre of a dramatic mix of hyperpop production and Arabic instruments. The result connects club aggression to longing and belonging.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: As Thoom, Zeynab Marwan joins producers Dylan Brady and Ike Clateman on a debut that brings hyperpop into contact with Arabic instrumentation. Her voice shifts from syrupy melody to a more menacing edge, and the review hears an artist moving beyond the more atmospheric approach of her earlier releases.

segments.title: Fury and feeling
segments.body: Tracks such as “Janani” and “On the Floor” build around forceful drums and mizmar, while “Morocco” uses oud and slower machines to frame a lover’s hurt. The review praises the way the production amplifies Marwan’s performances, though it finds some of the more conventional songs less distinctive.

The closing song, “I’m Going Back to Lebanon”, holds together a farewell to a lover and a desire to return to Marwan’s homeland. Its unanswered questions about return and renewed conflict give the album’s themes of attachment and uncertainty their clearest expression.

content.headline: R.E.M.’s Reveal reissue shows how a once-overlooked album shaped indie-pop
content.shortHeadline: R.E.M.’s Reveal reissue points toward indie-pop’s future
content.standfirst: The band’s 2001 move toward warm synth-pop, once overshadowed by its earlier work, sounds newly influential on a 25th-anniversary edition. The review also finds fresh life in a set of archival live performances.

sources.originalTitle: Reveal (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Recorded after drummer Bill Berry’s retirement, Reveal shifted R.E.M. toward a more reflective sound, with strings and electronics replacing some of the band’s earlier rock mysticism. The review argues the album’s dreamy, synth-pop arrangements now look like a precursor to later indie-pop.

segments.title: A reissue with room to roam
segments.body: The review singles out “All the Way to Reno (You’re Gonna Be a Star)” and “Imitation of Life”, while bonus material captures the expanded band playing for Radio France. Familiar songs take on different textures in performance, from organ in “So. Central Rain” to piano and massed vocals on “It’s the End of the World as We Know It (and I Feel Fine)”.

content.headline: Kim Deal’s Barbican concert album lets her personality shine through
content.shortHeadline: Kim Deal’s live album adds orchestral warmth to her songs
content.standfirst: A 13-piece orchestra and choir expand the arrangements from Kim Deal’s solo debut on this London concert recording. It is less a radical reinvention than an affectionate showcase for her distinctive voice.

sources.originalTitle: Live at the Barbican

segments.body: Recorded at London’s Barbican, the concert album draws mostly on Kim Deal’s solo debut, with a few earlier solo songs and Breeders material. The orchestral arrangements largely stay faithful to the studio versions, but the review finds that their strings and brass add subtle warmth and scale.

The orchestra makes a particular difference on “Beautiful Moon”, where cello gives the spare original a more haunting shape. The Shards choir is less prominent, but Deal herself takes centre stage: her rough-edged, expressive delivery brings vulnerability and force to “Walking With a Killer”.

content.headline: Threshold’s new folk-prog sound leads a week of adventurous tracks
content.shortHeadline: Threshold leads a week of adventurous new tracks
content.standfirst: Isaac Eiger’s solo project moves beyond the jangle-pop of Strange Ranger toward folk and loose, minimalist prog. The Guardian’s weekly picks also span experimental pop, UK rap, jazz and more.

image.caption: Threshold, Isaac Eiger’s solo project.

sources.originalTitle: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold

segments.body: Threshold’s “Stillwater” stretches out like a wintry walk, drawing on 1970s singer-songwriter piano ballads while pointing toward the wider sound of Isaac Eiger’s forthcoming debut album. The former Strange Ranger frontman’s new material reaches into traditional folk and minimalist prog, leaving his earlier jangle-pop behind.

segments.title: More to hear this week
segments.body: The roundup’s other picks include Heavensouls’ ten-minute experimental piece, a noirish collaboration from BexBlu and Paul Stephan, new tracks from Erika de Casier and Rema, and music by Studio20, Kacey Musgraves and Brazilian duo João Bosco and Guto Wirtti.

content.headline: Paul Schrader embraces AI for filmmaking, even as he fears what it may unleash
content.shortHeadline: Paul Schrader is using AI—and worries it could outgrow him
content.standfirst: The Taxi Driver writer is testing AI-generated actors, scripts and hallucinations for new projects. He sees the technology as hard to resist, but says asking it to write in his own style left him frightened by its capabilities.

image.caption: Paul Schrader, who is experimenting with AI in filmmaking.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m opening the cage of a monster’: Taxi Driver scriptwriter Paul Schrader on unleashing AI at 80

segments.body: At 80, Paul Schrader is using artificial intelligence to develop films, including horror-thriller The Doors of Perception, which will feature AI-generated psychedelic visions. He has also tested synthetic actors and says the technology could make a whole film, while giving him an unusually easy route around the costs and delays of conventional production.

segments.title: A tool that unsettled its user
segments.body: Schrader says an AI system proposed premises for a script in his style, then produced a scene-by-scene outline and a formatted opening scene. The speed and resemblance to his own writing startled him. “I realised it could write a Paul Schrader script. I got scared,” he said.

segments.title: Hollywood’s unresolved argument
segments.body: While unions and institutions have tried to set limits on AI in film, Schrader believes financial incentives will make it difficult to stop. He also voices a much broader fear that humans may have no lasting place in a world shaped by increasingly capable machines; what remains unclear is how audiences will respond to films made this way.

content.headline: Wicker’s knowingly sexist fairy tale turns a perfect husband into a provocation
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s impossible husband makes for a provocative comedy
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of twigs in this bawdy medieval fantasy. Its reviewer enjoys the comedy but questions the story’s vision of a partner whose own desires barely count.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a lonely fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman pays a basketmaker to create her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s woven creation is attentive, attractive and seemingly devoted to pleasing her, setting off lust, envy and alarm in the village around them.

segments.title: Fantasy with a sharp edge
segments.body: The review relishes the film’s bawdy humour and argues that its fantasy of a considerate partner responds to familiar inequalities in heterosexual relationships. But it also sees a troubling premise: the husband’s agency is barely explored, and his wife’s wishes take priority even when he objects.

The reviewer finds the film’s contradictions hard to dismiss—and ultimately enjoys it. Colman’s fisherwoman seems to want kindness rather than obedience, but the story’s deliberately excessive reversal raises a question it does not quite resolve: when devotion is built into a partner, can it be freely given?

content.headline: Josephine asks what happens after a child witnesses sexual violence
content.shortHeadline: Josephine explores a child’s trauma after witnessing rape
content.standfirst: Director Beth de Araújo draws on her own experience for a drama about an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape. The film’s approach has prompted debate over how cinema should depict sexual violence and protect young performers.

sources.originalTitle: 'The subject is still taboo': Shocking new film Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child's eyes

segments.body: In Josephine, an eight-year-old girl witnesses a rape in a park, an event that shapes the story of her and her parents, played by Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan. Writer-director Beth de Araújo says the film draws on her own childhood experience and asks how a young person might understand violence before having words for it.

segments.title: Questions about showing violence
segments.body: The film depicts the assault from a distance through the child’s perspective. Film scholar Tanya Horeck says there is no single feminist rule for representing rape on screen, but asks what a scene is doing and whose perspective it serves. She finds the case for placing the scene early in Josephine compelling because the film follows the child’s trauma.

segments.title: Protecting a young actor
segments.body: Reeves, who was eight during filming, did not read the script or appear during the assault scene, and has not seen the finished film. De Araújo says a child psychologist was available to the family and that Reeves can choose whether to watch the film when she is 18.

content.headline: Oobah Butler’s pranks expose how easily industries can be gamed
content.shortHeadline: Oobah Butler turns industry loopholes into comedy
content.standfirst: In a new series, the prankster infiltrates sectors from wellness to music, testing their appetite for bogus products and manufactured hype. The review finds the stunts funny—and an unsettling look at gullibility and weak regulation.

image.caption: Oobah Butler in Scams for a Better Tomorrow.

sources.originalTitle: Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow review – these audacious pranks are tell-your-friends funny

segments.body: Oobah Butler’s five-part series takes his stunts inside industries including wellness, wine, dating, music and royalty. He sells fake wellness products, markets smoke-damaged wine at a premium and tries to make a machine-written song trend, presenting the schemes as experiments as well as jokes.

segments.title: The joke has a target
segments.body: The review praises Butler’s boldness and argues that his pranks mostly take aim at institutions rather than individuals. A former Theranos executive even appears to advise him on marketing, a pointed detail in a show about how readily dubious claims can be sold.

Behind the comic set-ups, the series finds loopholes, weak regulation and investors willing to back far-fetched schemes. The review’s broader verdict is that Butler’s pranks are both disquieting and unexpectedly reassuring: they expose how easily systems can be exploited, while making their targets laughable.

content.headline: The BBC is putting some Christmas specials on iPlayer weeks early
content.shortHeadline: The BBC is moving some Christmas TV specials earlier
content.standfirst: Several festive programmes will arrive on iPlayer from 27 November, ahead of their television broadcasts. The BBC says a longer streaming window reflects viewing habits, while the change leaves questions about the shared ritual of Christmas TV.

image.caption: Mary Berry filming her Christmas Countdown.

sources.originalTitle: ‘In the office, there was a sharp intake of breath’: why has the BBC decided to celebrate Christmas earlier than ever?

segments.body: The BBC plans to make several Christmas specials available on iPlayer from 27 November, in some cases almost a month before they air on television. The broadcaster says viewing of festive programmes has grown earlier in the season and that the longer window may help programmes find an audience.

segments.title: A change to a shared schedule
segments.body: Some major Christmas broadcasts, including the Strictly special and the new Call the Midwife prequel, remain scheduled for television as usual. Radio Times editor Shem Law says the earlier streaming releases may nevertheless weaken the appeal of gathering around a programme together when it finally airs.

content.headline: Melania’s two-part TV documentary offers little beyond its subject’s image
content.shortHeadline: Melania’s TV documentary is more advert than series
content.standfirst: A review finds the two short episodes almost empty of substance, apart from a brief encounter with people affected by natural disasters. The programme repeatedly turns its attention back to Melania Trump and her projects.

image.caption: Melania Trump.

sources.originalTitle: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space

segments.body: The review describes Melania as two episodes of short, disconnected scenes rather than a substantial series. It criticises the programme’s polished footage and vague statements, including an extended sequence in which Melania Trump considers the placement of a brooch.

A visit with people affected by Hurricane Helene and wildfires briefly shifts the programme toward their experiences. But the review says it soon returns to Trump’s own initiatives, leaving little room for the people the series appears to be documenting.

content.headline: I Am Helen puts the consequences of toxic masculinity in the foreground
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen shows the cost of toxic masculinity for women
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan plays a woman whose partner’s coercive behaviour escalates in the latest instalment of Dominic Savage’s drama anthology. The review argues that the series centres the women who are often overlooked in stories about male violence.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: Helen, played by Nicola Coughlan, is in a seemingly ordinary relationship until her partner Steve chokes her without consent during sex. The review focuses on the aftermath: he presents himself as the victim, and Helen ends up apologising before their life returns to normal.

segments.title: The violence of the everyday
segments.body: The review argues that the drama’s disturbing force comes from how ordinary Steve’s behaviour can seem. His grievances about masculinity are reinforced by a friend and grow into coercion and anger, while Helen recognises the pattern but struggles to make him listen.

Rather than centre the destructive man, the episode makes the consequences for his partner its focus. The review sees this shift as an important contribution to television’s treatment of toxic masculinity, while stressing that men’s insecurity does not erase the harm women experience.

content.headline: Black Doves returns with Keira Knightley’s conflicted spy at its centre
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves returns to its mix of violence and feeling
content.standfirst: The cast and creator discuss the Netflix thriller’s second season, where Helen faces new risks as her husband nears Downing Street. Its murderous antiheroes, they say, work because the show keeps their humour and humanity in view.

image.caption: Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Keira Knightley returns as Helen Webb, a spy whose marriage to a politician is bound up with her work for the Black Doves organisation. In the new season, she searches for her missing handler while facing the consequences of her husband’s rise to No 10.

segments.title: Violence with consequences
segments.body: Knightley says the show’s violence can feel like a video game before a sudden moment brings the human cost into focus. Creator Joe Barton says the series tries to acknowledge how violence is normalised in spy stories, even as it asks viewers to care about characters who have killed many people.

Ambika Mod joins as Laila Joshi, a rogue agent who becomes an uneasy ally to Helen. Knightley describes the women’s relationship as an entertaining mix of antagonism and dependence, while Barton says the new season was difficult to shape after several versions of its opening episode.

content.headline: A week’s streaming picks include a new Blade Runner series and Oobah Butler
content.shortHeadline: What to stream: Blade Runner 2099, Oobah Butler and more
content.standfirst: A new Blade Runner miniseries and Oobah Butler’s prank-driven show lead this week’s selection, alongside a Buffalo blizzard documentary, Jennifer Lopez in concert and a BBC Christmas ghost story.

image.caption: Michelle Yeoh as Olwen and Hunter Schafer as Cora in Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099 to Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: Blade Runner 2099 brings Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer to a new story in the franchise, while Oobah Butler’s latest series takes his elaborate hoaxes into different industries. Both are among the Guardian’s picks for new films and programmes to stream this week.

segments.title: More to watch
segments.body: The selection also includes a partly animated documentary about a community sheltering together during a deadly Buffalo blizzard, Jennifer Lopez’s Las Vegas concert film, and a BBC adaptation of a Charles Dickens ghost story. The listings provide a range of options across streaming services and broadcast television.

content.headline: GTA VI claims a record launch, with Rockstar reporting $3.79bn in first-day US$
content.shortHeadline: Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79bn on launch day
content.standfirst: Rockstar says Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, a figure that would make the game’s launch exceptionally large across entertainment. The company’s estimate has not been independently verified in the supplied reporting.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says

segments.body: Rockstar Games says Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, based on the company’s estimates through the end of launch day. The publisher calls it the biggest entertainment launch in history; that comparison is Rockstar’s claim.

segments.title: A record-setting release
segments.body: Rockstar says 32.5 million copies had been sold before release, and that the launch figure is nearly five times the first-day sales reported for GTA V in 2013. The game went on sale for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

The same report notes that police departments urged the public not to imitate the game’s car thefts and other crimes in real life. It also says there is insufficient evidence of a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psychological Association.

content.headline: Elden Ring’s film adaptation faces the challenge of making its world matter
content.shortHeadline: Can an Elden Ring film make its vast world matter?
content.standfirst: Alex Garland’s adaptation has a reported budget near $200m and a major cast, but the game’s horror-tinged fantasy world is not a story by itself. The feature weighs the challenge of giving its setting a reason to hold an audience.

image.caption: A scene from Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: The Guardian’s feature treats Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation as an unusually high-stakes attempt to bring a vast game world to cinema. The film is reported to be in post-production, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Nick Offerman; its budget is said to be close to $200m.

segments.title: A world is not a story
segments.body: The article points to earlier fantasy adaptations that struggled to turn elaborate settings into compelling films. Elden Ring’s landscape is especially grim, populated by grotesque creatures and survivors living amid death, leaving open questions about who audiences will follow and what the film’s narrative will be.

Leaked images have prompted speculation that the film may draw on events before the game, but the feature presents that as a possibility rather than a confirmed approach. Garland’s history of resisting conventional reassurance may suit the material, though the scale of the reported budget raises questions about how much freedom he will have.

content.headline: GTA VI is not for children, despite its appeal as a blockbuster game
content.shortHeadline: Why GTA VI’s 18 rating matters for parents
content.standfirst: The review praises Rockstar’s ambitious game but details its explicit sex, drugs and violence. Its central advice to parents is straightforward: the 18 rating signals adult content, not a difficulty level.

sources.originalTitle: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child

segments.body: The Guardian’s reviewer calls Grand Theft Auto VI an impressive and sometimes touching game, but says it is among the most explicit they have played. Its crime story includes graphic violence, full-frontal nudity, sex scenes and extensive drug use.

segments.title: A rating is a content warning
segments.body: The piece describes sexual material in the main story and in optional settings, alongside adult dialogue on the game’s fictional radio and television. The reviewer’s concern is not that adults should avoid such content, but that parents may mistake an 18 rating for a measure of difficulty rather than a warning about subject matter.

After more than 70 hours with the game, the reviewer’s advice is that it is not suitable for young children. The article suggests parents consider whether they would let their child watch Breaking Bad, while recognising that older teenagers’ experiences and maturity differ.

content.headline: Keepsake County turns suburban burglary into a melancholy stealth game
content.shortHeadline: Keepsake County makes a lonely life of theft playable
content.standfirst: This small stealth game sends a debt-ridden burglar through garish Midwestern homes, where even the loot can be a half-eaten pizza or cheap ornament. Its comic oddities sit alongside a bleak account of financial precarity.

image.caption: A scene from Keepsake County.

sources.originalTitle: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience

segments.body: In Keepsake County, Samuel breaks into suburban homes and steals what he can carry, from golf clubs to half-eaten food. He avoids killing residents, instead tying them up with improvised restraints, and takes his haul to a pawn shop rather than building a conventional arsenal of upgrades.

segments.title: Comedy with a hard edge
segments.body: The review likens the game’s eccentric art and bleak humour to a low-budget television comedy, while noting how Samuel’s medical debts and legal fees make each break-in feel less like a route to success than an act of survival. Its quiet loading-screen landscapes reinforce the character’s isolation.

The game’s repetitive robberies can feel one-note, and the review notes repeated dialogue and limited differences between regions. Yet it argues that the repetition also gives the routine its melancholy force: Samuel has little chance of escaping the conditions that keep sending him back into other people’s homes.

content.headline: Union says it has lost confidence in UK science funder over planned cuts
content.shortHeadline: Union loses confidence in UK science funder over planned cuts
content.standfirst: Prospect says UKRI’s cost-saving plans could damage national science capability and were launched without proper consultation. UKRI’s board and the science minister say they back its chief executive and reform programme.

image.caption: Jodrell Bank Observatory, whose future is at risk under planned UKRI funding changes.

sources.originalTitle: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts

segments.body: Prospect, a union representing scientists and engineers, says it has lost confidence in Ian Chapman, chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), over planned cuts and changes to research facilities. General secretary Mike Clancy urged UKRI to pause its voluntary exit scheme and consult unions on the potential impact.

segments.title: What is at stake
segments.body:
The Science and Technology Facilities Council, part of UKRI, needs to save £162m by 2030. Plans put the future of the UK’s largest telescope at Jodrell Bank at risk, while the Clara accelerator facility is to be mothballed. Other facilities, including Diamond Light Source, are expected to make efficiency savings.

UKRI says it has engaged with staff and research communities and must keep costs within its budget. Its chair, Leszek Borysiewicz, and science minister Chris McDonald both expressed confidence in Chapman and defended the programme as a way to focus resources and deliver value for money.

content.headline: UK hospitals prepare to use Alzheimer’s blood tests before trials conclude
content.shortHeadline: Alzheimer’s blood tests set to reach more UK hospitals
content.standfirst: Some hospitals are introducing a test that may help identify Alzheimer’s within days of a memory-clinic visit, rather than after months or years. Trials are still under way, and access may vary by location.

image.caption: A blood test could help doctors assess people with memory problems for Alzheimer’s.

sources.originalTitle: Blood tests that cut Alzheimer’s diagnosis from years to days coming in early 2027

segments.body: A number of UK hospitals are preparing to offer blood tests for Alzheimer’s as part of routine care, with Manchester Brain Health Centre expecting to start within weeks. The test measures a form of tau protein, ptau217, and may help clinicians distinguish Alzheimer’s from other causes of memory problems. University College Hospital in London is already offering it.

segments.title: Earlier diagnosis, uneven access
segments.body:
A faster result could help people and their families plan and may allow some patients to access treatment or clinical trials sooner. Two large trials assessing how the tests fit into NHS services are not due to finish until 2029; hospitals can introduce them earlier, but there is no central register of providers.

That leaves a potential postcode lottery. Doctors also caution that tests bought privately outside a memory-clinic assessment could produce false positives. A blood result is part of a clinical assessment, not a standalone diagnosis.

content.headline: Climate scientists clash over a proposed delay to the IPCC’s next report
content.shortHeadline: Dispute over timing and representation delays IPCC report
content.standfirst: Some governments want the IPCC’s next assessment delayed until after a key climate stocktake, while other countries and scientists warn that a hold-up could weaken global cooperation. The dispute also centres on representation and whose assumptions shape the analysis.

sources.originalTitle: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist

segments.body: The IPCC’s next assessment is under way and is hoped to be completed in 2028, in time to inform the 2028 global stocktake under the Paris agreement. Russia, India and the Arab group, including Saudi Arabia, have argued for publication in 2029 instead, saying developing countries are disadvantaged in the process and that some of its assumptions favour richer nations.

segments.title: A dispute about evidence and equity
segments.body:
Potsdam Institute director Johan Rockström says the assessment is an objective synthesis of peer-reviewed research and should not be delayed. Other developing countries, including small island states and least-developed countries, have also called for the work to proceed. The IPCC says 51% of the 664 appointed authors for its three reports come from developing countries and economies in transition.

Lidy Nacpil of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development argues that some emissions-cutting scenarios are biased against the global south, including by assuming that reductions should be made where they are cheapest.
